newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB's Meyer says policy has not changed.
newsitem.headline: SNB's Meyer says policy has not changed.

text.p: Hans Meyer, president of the Swiss National Bank (SNB), said the central bank had not changed its basic policy and it was long-standing practice to take other indicators into account when there were difficulties in following the main indicator, seasonally-adjusted central money supply.
Meyer also said in an interview with the Basler Zeitung that there was room for a slight decline in Swiss nominal interest rates following last week's cut in the discount rate.
Asked whether nominal interest rates could ease further, Meyer said: "That is conceivable. But there should not be much more room," Meyer said.
Seasonally-adjusted central bank money comprises notes in circulation plus banks' deposits at the SNB.
The SNB's cut in its discount rate to 1.0 percent last week was seen by some economists as a sign the bank's monetary policy was based on an exchange rate policy rather than money supply.
"It is often said that we are following a new policy. Of course, we are not following any new policy, just carrying out our concepts in a changed environment," Meyer said.
He added that one aspect of the current environment was that the SNB lately had trouble with transparency of money supply.
In such cases, the long-standing practice of the SNB is to look at other indicators, such as the broader monetary aggregates, interest rates and exchange rates.

Tightness in Swiss money markets in July and August was largely due to a technical shift in the holdings of commercial banks when they moved funds from the Swiss Post Bank into their accounts at the SNB.
The rise in Swiss money rates coincided with an appreciation of the Swiss franc.
Meyer also said the SNB has been accused of never taking any other factors into account than the money supply.
"But we have always looked at markets to see that they develop in an organic manner," Meyer said.

Since the abolition of fixed exchange rates in the early 1970s, the SNB has oriented its monetary policy to money supply targets under the assumption that there is a correlation between money supply and price stability.
The bank, however, has not always achieved its targets because it has been willing to deviate to take into account exceptional events.

Such events include the introduction of Value-Added-Tax (VAT) and the SNB has also in many cases reacted to strong exchange fluctuations. In 1978, for example, the bank inflated the money supply to counteract a strong appreciation of the Swiss franc.
